prompt: Which of the following statements are true for a centralized network architecture? (6p)
options: The access point/base station controls medium access.
Nodes normally communicate with the access point using single-hop links.
5G and LoRa networks are examples of centralized architectures.
Nodes organize themselves without any central controller.
A centralized architecture always requires multi-hop communication.
ZigBee mesh is a purely centralized architecture.
A gateway is never needed in a centralized network.
The base station can coordinate when nodes transmit.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 8. False: 4, 5, 6, 7.

Centralized means that a base station/AP coordinates the nodes; direct single-hop access is typical. ZigBee mesh is decentralized, and a gateway is still needed for Internet connectivity.

prompt: Which of the following statements are true for a decentralized network architecture? (6p)
options: Nodes can organize themselves without a fixed base station.
Multi-hop forwarding is common in decentralized networks.
BLE Mesh and ZigBee mesh are decentralized architectures.
A central access point controls all medium access.
Decentralized networks always use single-hop communication.
Routing is never needed in a decentralized network.
All decentralized networks are time-critical.
Nodes can communicate directly with each other.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 8. False: 4, 5, 6, 7.

Ad-hoc and mesh networks are self-organized and often multi-hop. Routing is an important part of multi-hop decentralized networks.

prompt: Which statements are true for a wireless mesh network? (6p)
options: Mesh nodes can forward data for other nodes.
A portal connects the mesh to the Internet.
Hosts can connect to the mesh via any mesh node.
A mesh network can only have one node.
Mesh networks never use routing.
Mesh nodes must always be mobile.
A mesh network is always a DTN.
Data can travel over multiple hops before reaching the portal.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 8. False: 4, 5, 6, 7.

Mesh nodes provide forwarding and path selection; the portal is the Internet gateway. Hosts communicate through mesh nodes.

prompt: Which statements are true for personal area networks (PAN)? (6p)
options: BLE is intended for non-critical applications.
ZigBee can form a mesh network.
BLE Mesh uses relay nodes to extend coverage.
BLE only supports single-hop communication.
ZigBee requires a cellular base station.
Bluetooth uses frequency hopping in the 2.4 GHz band.
ZigBee has no coordinator node.
PAN technologies are typically short-range.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 6, 8. False: 4, 5, 7.

BLE Mesh is decentralized and multi-hop. ZigBee uses a coordinator and a mesh; Bluetooth classic uses frequency hopping.

prompt: Which statements are true for LPWAN technologies? (6p)
options: LoRa is designed for long range and low energy.
NB-IoT uses licensed cellular spectrum.
LoRaWAN uses gateways and a network server.
LoRa typically provides very high data rates.
NB-IoT is a decentralized ad-hoc technology.
LTE-M is a cellular LPWAN variant.
LPWAN is aimed at resource-constrained devices.
LoRa requires a licensed frequency band.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7. False: 4, 5, 8.

LPWAN trades data rate for range and energy. LoRa is used in unlicensed bands; NB-IoT/LTE-M are cellular and centralized.
source_label: Källa: Low-Power-Wide-Area-Networks-LPWAN.pdf s. 10 · Artiklar: Rashmi Sharan Sinha · Semtech

prompt: Which statements are true for WiFi 6/7 mesh? (6p)
options: OFDMA can be used for more efficient channel access.
MU-MIMO allows an access point to serve multiple users simultaneously.
A mesh portal connects the mesh to the Internet.
HWMP is a path-selection protocol for WiFi mesh.
WiFi mesh always uses a single-hop architecture.
MCCA is a contention-free mesh channel access mechanism.
WiFi 6/7 is a delay-tolerant networking technology.
WiFi mesh has no routing function.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6. False: 5, 7, 8.

WiFi 6/7 adds OFDMA and MU-MIMO. Mesh uses HWMP for path selection and MCCA for coordinated access; it is not a DTN.
source_label: Källa: IEEE-802.11-WiFi.pdf s. 1 · Artiklar: David López-Pérez · Boris Bellalta

prompt: Which statements are true for 5G and C-RAN? (6p)
options: URLLC targets very low latency and high reliability.
eMBB targets high data rates.
mMTC targets massive numbers of low-power devices.
C-RAN separates the BBU from the remote radio heads.
Network slicing can create logically separate networks.
C-RAN places the BBU in every base station.
5G can only be used for satellite communication.
Network slicing requires a separate physical antenna for every user.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. False: 6, 7, 8.

C-RAN centralizes BBUs and distributes RRHs. Slicing is logical, not a separate antenna per user.
source_label: Källa: Cellular-Mobile-Networks.pdf s. 1 · Artiklar: Ericsson · Aleksandra Checko

prompt: Which statements are true for satellite/NTN systems? (6p)
options: Starlink is a LEO broadband system often used as backhaul.
Argos is aimed at low-rate, resource-constrained sensors.
Iridium provides global voice and data via LEO satellites.
LEO satellites generally have lower delay than GEO satellites.
Argos provides high-rate full-duplex video.
Starlink is designed only for one-way telemetry.
GEO satellites are always closer to Earth than LEO satellites.
Satellite links can be used where terrestrial coverage is missing.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 4, 8. False: 5, 6, 7.

Argos is low-rate telemetry; Starlink is broadband. LEO is closer than GEO.
source_label: Källa: Non-Terrestrial-Networks-NTN.pdf s. 13 · Artiklar: Oltjon Kodheli · Carles Gomez

prompt: Which statements are true for delay-tolerant networking (DTN)? (6p)
options: DTN uses store-and-forward.
Bundle protocol is a DTN protocol.
DTN protocols are implemented as an overlay, often above the transport layer.
DTN requires a continuous end-to-end connection.
DTN is suitable for non-critical applications.
LTP is a DTN protocol for long-delay links.
DTN only supports single-hop communication.
DTN is always time-critical.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6. False: 4, 7, 8.

DTN tolerates intermittent links by storing data until the next contact. LTP and Bundle are DTN protocols; it is not for hard real-time traffic.
source_label: Källa: Delay-tolerant-networking.pdf s. 1 · Artikel: Forrest Warthman

prompt: Which statements are true for underwater wireless networks? (6p)
options: Acoustic communication can provide long range but low data rate.
Optical communication requires approximately line-of-sight.
JANUS is an underwater acoustic communication standard.
GPS works well for localization underwater.
Radio communication at high frequencies has very long underwater range.
AUVs can act as mobile nodes in underwater networks.
Underwater networks can use DTN solutions.
Acoustic communication has lower propagation delay than radio in air.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7. False: 4, 5, 8.

GPS radio does not penetrate water well. Acoustic waves travel slowly compared with radio; JANUS is an acoustic standard.
source_label: Källa: Underwater-networks.pdf s. 13 · Artiklar: Camila M. G. Gussen · Huimin Lu

prompt: Which statements are true for cloud, edge, fog and CDN? (6p)
options: Edge computing moves computation closer to users.
A CDN caches content closer to users.
Fog computing distributes cloud-like resources closer to the edge.
A CDN is exactly the same thing as fog computing.
Cloud computing provides on-demand resources over a network.
Edge computing always means a central data center.
Fog computing eliminates the need for any network.
CDNs can reduce latency and network load.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. False: 4, 6, 7.

Fog is broader than CDN; CDN is a content-caching architecture. Edge is near the user, not central.
source_label: Källa: Users-and-back-ends.pdf s. 16 · Artiklar: William Tärneberg · Huda S. Goian

prompt: Which statements are true for queueing models? (6p)
options: For M/M/1, utilization is ρ = λ/μ.
A stable single-server system requires λ < μ.
Little's law is N = λT.
M/M/1 has deterministic service times.
M/D/1 has deterministic service times.
Throughput is always λ, even when requests are blocked.
Utilization can exceed 1 in a stable system.
The Pollaczek-Khinchine formula is used for M/G/1.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. False: 4, 6, 7.

M/M/1 has exponential service; M/D/1 has deterministic service. With blocking, effective throughput is lower than λ.

prompt: Which statements are true for routing in ad-hoc networks? (6p)
options: AODV is a reactive routing protocol.
Position-based routing uses node positions.
Geocast sends a message to nodes in a geographic area.
AODV is a proactive protocol that always maintains all routes.
Geocast is a unicast protocol to one fixed node.
Multi-hop routing can forward data through intermediate nodes.
Position-based routing never needs position information.
Broadcast sends a message to all reachable nodes.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 6, 8. False: 4, 5, 7.

AODV discovers routes on demand. Geocast targets a zone; broadcast floods to all reachable nodes.

prompt: Which statements are true for resource-constrained networking? (6p)
options: Devices often have limited energy and computing power.
LoRa and NB-IoT can be suitable technologies.
Multi-hop communication can extend coverage.
Resource-constrained devices always have mains power.
WiFi 6 is always the best choice for battery-powered sensors.
Energy-efficient MAC protocols are important.
Resource-constrained networking is the same thing as DTN.
Low data rate can be an acceptable trade-off for long battery life.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 6, 8. False: 4, 5, 7.

Resource constraints drive low-power MAC and LPWAN choices; DTN is a different concept.

prompt: Which statements are true for space communication? (6p)
options: Deep-space links can have very long propagation delays.
A space relay can forward a link when there is no direct line of sight.
Optical and radio communication can be used in space.
Acoustic communication is commonly used between planets.
Spacecraft often rely on solar power.
DTN concepts can be useful for space networks.
Space links always have very low delay.
A space relay is always a base station on a planet.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6. False: 4, 7, 8.

Space relays are satellites that bend/forward links; acoustic communication is not used in space.
source_label: Källa: Interplanetary-networks.pdf s. 1 · Artikel: Kanglian Zhao

prompt:
A server receives requests as a Poisson process with λ = 8 requests/s. Service times are exponential with mean 0.08 s. Model it as M/M/1 with an unlimited queue.

  1. What is the utilization?
  2. What is the throughput?
  3. What is the average number of requests in the system?
  4. What is the average response time?
solution:
Solution

μ = 1/0.08 = 12.5 requests/s. ρ = λ/μ = 8/12.5 = 0.64.

Throughput = λ = 8 requests/s (no blocking).

For M/M/1: N = ρ/(1−ρ) = 0.64/0.36 ≈ 1.78 requests.

Little: T = N/λ = 1.78/8 ≈ 0.222 s.

prompt:
Repeat the previous system, but assume deterministic service times with the same mean 0.08 s. Model it as M/D/1.

  1. What is the utilization?
  2. What is the average number of requests in the system?
  3. What is the average response time?

Data packets arrive as a Poisson process with λ = 3 packets/s.

  1. What is the probability of exactly 4 arrivals during 2 seconds?
  2. What is the probability of zero arrivals during 1 second?
  3. What is the expected number of arrivals during 4 seconds?
solution:
Solution

For 2 s, mean = 6: P(N=4) = e−664/4! ≈ 0.1339.

For 1 s, mean = 3: P(N=0) = e−3 ≈ 0.0498.

For 4 s, expected number = 3·4 = 12.

prompt:
Four devices use slotted ALOHA. In each slot, A and B transmit with probability 0.2 and C and D with probability 0.3, independently. Assume a frame is successful only if exactly one device transmits.

  1. What is the probability that a slot is empty?
  2. What is the probability of exactly one transmission?
  3. What is the probability of a collision?

A ground station sends a 10 kbit message to the Moon over a 1 Mbit/s link. The distance is 384,400 km and the signal travels at 3·108 m/s. Ignore processing and queueing.

  1. What is the propagation delay?
  2. What is the transmission time?
  3. What is the total one-way delay?
solution:
Solution

Propagation: 384,400,000 / 3·108 ≈ 1.281 s.

Transmission: 10,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.01 s.

Total = 1.281 + 0.01 ≈ 1.291 s.

prompt:
A queueing system has at most 3 requests. Measurements give P(0)=0.19, P(1)=0.23, P(2)=0.26 and P(3)=0.32. New requests arrive with λ = 4 requests/s and are blocked if the system is full. Service rate is μ = 5 requests/s.

  1. What is the average number of requests in the system?
  2. What is the blocking probability?
  3. What is the effective throughput?
  4. What is the average response time for accepted requests?
solution:
Solution

N = 0·0.19 + 1·0.23 + 2·0.26 + 3·0.32 = 1.71.

Blocking probability = P(3) = 0.32.

λeff = λ(1 − Pblock) = 4·0.68 = 2.72 requests/s.

Little: T = N/λeff = 1.71/2.72 ≈ 0.629 s.

prompt: Scenario: A 12-storey hospital wants to track about 1000 medical carts. The most important requirement is to know which floor a cart is on. The building has WiFi and wired Internet. Propose an end-to-end network system and motivate your choices.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use a low-power indoor technology such as BLE or ZigBee with anchors on each floor; tags on the carts.
  • Anchors form a centralized or mesh network and forward data to floor gateways.
  • Gateways use the hospital LAN/WiFi as backhaul to a cloud/back-end service.
  • Floor-level accuracy is sufficient, so RSSI/trilateration can be used; no GPS is needed indoors.
  • Consider battery life, privacy, and redundancy; 1000 devices require capacity planning.

prompt: Scenario: A farm wants to monitor 20 cows with hourly position updates. The pasture is large and cellular coverage is weak. Data should reach a cloud service. Propose a complete network system.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use battery/solar-powered LPWAN tags (LoRa or NB-IoT if coverage exists).
  • Deploy a LoRa gateway with backhaul (fiber/4G/satellite) to the Internet.
  • Send data to a cloud back-end for storage and visualization.
  • Use duty cycling/energy-efficient MAC; hourly updates are non-critical.
  • If no gateway coverage, use a DTN/mobile gateway for store-and-forward.
source_label: Källa: Low-Power-Wide-Area-Networks-LPWAN.pdf s. 4 · Artikel: Rashmi Sharan Sinha

prompt: Scenario: Monitor oil spills around offshore platforms. You have underwater sensors, AUVs, small boats and a cloud server. Design an end-to-end system.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use acoustic links for long-range underwater sensor data; optical links for short high-rate AUV transfers.
  • JANUS can provide an interoperable acoustic MAC.
  • AUVs collect data from sensors and carry it to surface gateways/boats (DTN/store-and-forward).
  • Surface nodes use satellite or cellular backhaul to the cloud.
  • Localization cannot rely on GPS underwater; use acoustic ranging or known positions.
source_label: Källa: Underwater-networks.pdf s. 25 · Artiklar: Camila M. G. Gussen · Huimin Lu

prompt: Scenario: Environmental sensors are spread over a remote region with no terrestrial network. Design a satellite-based monitoring system with low maintenance and low energy use.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use Argos or a similar low-rate satellite IoT system for small, infrequent sensor messages.
  • Use Starlink or another broadband satellite link for a local gateway if higher data rates are needed.
  • Solar panels and batteries plus DRX/duty cycling reduce energy use.
  • Satellite links provide backhaul to a cloud back-end.
  • Store-and-forward/DTN can handle intermittent contacts.
source_label: Källa: Non-Terrestrial-Networks-NTN.pdf s. 24 · Artiklar: Oltjon Kodheli · Carles Gomez

prompt: Scenario: A humanitarian emergency has destroyed the terrestrial network. Relief teams need local communication and a link to the Internet. Design a network architecture.
solution:
Example solution

  • Deploy a rapidly installable WiFi/mesh network for local teams.
  • Use satellite backhaul (Starlink/VSAT) at a gateway/portal.
  • Use DTN/store-and-forward for intermittent links and delay-tolerant data.
  • Prioritize voice, messaging and sensor data; use edge/fog processing locally.
  • Power via generators/solar and plan for limited capacity.
source_label: Källa: Delay-tolerant-networking.pdf s. 1 · Artikel: Forrest Warthman

prompt: Scenario: A factory wants private 5G for AGVs and robots with low latency, plus massive sensor data and video. Design the network and explain the role of edge computing.
solution:
Example solution

  • Deploy a private 5G network or a dedicated slice of a public 5G network.
  • Use URLLC for robot control and eMBB for video; mMTC for sensors.
  • Place edge computing near the factory to reduce latency.
  • Use a local backhaul and redundant links; integrate with the factory IT/OT network.
  • Plan security, isolation and coverage indoors.
source_label: Källa: Cellular-Mobile-Networks.pdf s. 1 · Artikel: Hyoungju Ji

prompt: Which statements are true for basic networked systems? (6p)
options: A host sends and receives data via a network link.
A gateway connects two networks or a local network to the Internet.
All nodes in a local network always need a global IP address.
Time-critical applications typically need low latency.
Non-critical applications can tolerate more delay.
A backhaul link connects an access network to the core/Internet.
A router and a host are always the same thing.
Physical/MAC addresses are used within a local network.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8. False: 3, 7.

Nodes behind a gateway can use private/local addresses; routers forward between networks, while hosts are endpoints.

prompt: Which statements are true for ad-hoc MAC and routing? (6p)
options: Contention-based MAC allows nodes to compete for the medium.
The hidden terminal problem can cause collisions at the receiver.
AODV discovers routes on demand.
Contention-free MAC completely eliminates the need for scheduling.
RTS/CTS can help with the hidden terminal problem.
Geocast sends data to a geographic zone.
All ad-hoc networks must use a central base station.
Broadcast sends data to all reachable nodes.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8. False: 4, 7.

Contention-free MAC requires scheduling/coordination. Ad-hoc networks do not need a central base station.

prompt: Which statements are true for backhaul, positioning and power? (6p)
options: Fiber and radio links can be used as backhaul.
A gateway can connect a local network to the Internet.
GPS works well indoors for all sensor nodes.
Battery and solar power are common for remote sensors.
Mains power is always available in sensor networks.
The backhaul link can be a bottleneck.
Localization can use radio signal strength or acoustic ranging.
A sensor network never needs a power source.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7. False: 3, 5, 8.

GPS is unreliable indoors. Remote sensors often use batteries/solar, and backhaul capacity must be planned.

prompt: Which statements compare LoRa and NB-IoT correctly? (6p)
options: LoRa can operate in unlicensed bands.
NB-IoT uses licensed cellular spectrum.
LoRa is typically centralized around gateways.
NB-IoT is designed for very high data rates.
Both are aimed at low-power, long-range IoT.
NB-IoT is a decentralized ad-hoc technology.
LoRa supports different device classes with different receive behavior.
LTE-M is a cellular LPWAN technology.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8. False: 4, 6.

NB-IoT is cellular and centralized. LPWAN technologies trade data rate for range and energy.

prompt: Which statements compare BLE and ZigBee correctly? (6p)
options: BLE Mesh is decentralized and supports multi-hop.
ZigBee is based on IEEE 802.15.4.
ZigBee networks use a coordinator.
BLE Mesh requires a central hub for all traffic.
ZigBee can form a mesh network.
BLE is intended for time-critical industrial control by default.
Both are PAN technologies aimed at short-range communication.
ZigBee uses frequency hopping in the 60 GHz band.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 7. False: 4, 6, 8.

BLE Mesh has no central hub; ZigBee uses a coordinator. Both are short-range PAN technologies.

prompt: Which statements are true for the WiFi mesh architecture? (6p)
options: A portal is the mesh node connected to the Internet.
Hosts connect to the mesh through a mesh node.
HWMP provides path selection.
MCCA is a coordinated channel access mechanism.
All mesh nodes must be connected by fiber.
Mesh nodes can forward data for other mesh nodes.
WiFi mesh is a delay-tolerant network by definition.
The mesh can use multi-hop forwarding.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8. False: 5, 7.

WiFi mesh uses wireless mesh links, HWMP and MCCA. It is not a DTN by definition.

prompt: Which statements are true for C-RAN and network slicing? (6p)
options: C-RAN centralizes BBUs and distributes RRHs.
Network slicing can isolate resources for different services.
URLLC is a 5G service class for low latency.
C-RAN requires a separate physical network for every user.
mMTC is aimed at massive numbers of devices.
eMBB is aimed at high data rates.
Network slicing is only possible in WiFi.
A private 5G network can use a dedicated slice.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8. False: 4, 7.

Slicing is logical. C-RAN separates BBU/RRH; 5G defines eMBB, URLLC and mMTC.

prompt: Which statements are true for satellite IoT? (6p)
options: Argos is suitable for low-rate sensor telemetry.
Starlink is a LEO broadband system.
Iridium uses inter-satellite links.
Argos is designed for high-rate video streaming.
LEO satellites typically have lower delay than GEO.
Satellite links can provide backhaul in remote areas.
GPS is a satellite navigation system, not a communication backhaul.
All satellite systems provide free global Internet.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7. False: 4, 8.

Argos is low-rate; Starlink/Iridium are broadband/voice-data systems. Satellite coverage can be used as backhaul.

prompt: Which statements are true for DTN in space? (6p)
options: Deep-space links can have minutes of propagation delay.
Store-and-forward is central to DTN.
LTP can be used for long-delay space links.
Bundle protocol is a DTN protocol.
DTN requires continuous end-to-end connectivity.
A space relay can help when there is no direct line of sight.
TCP is always the best transport protocol for deep space.
Contacts may be scheduled in advance.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8. False: 5, 7.

DTN tolerates intermittent links; TCP's assumptions do not fit long-delay space paths.

prompt: Which statements are true for underwater communication technologies? (6p)
options: Acoustic links can cover long ranges at low data rates.
Optical links can provide high rates over short line-of-sight distances.
RF links can be used underwater but are strongly attenuated.
JANUS is an acoustic communication standard.
GPS works well at depth.
AUVs can act as mobile data mules.
Acoustic communication has very low propagation delay.
Multi-hop underwater networks are impossible.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6. False: 5, 7, 8.

GPS is unavailable underwater. Acoustic propagation is slow compared with radio; multi-hop and DTN can be used.

prompt: Which statements are true for performance metrics? (6p)
options: Utilization is the fraction of time the server is busy.
Throughput is the average departure rate.
Response time includes queueing and service time.
Little's law applies only to M/M/1.
A stable queue requires demand below capacity.
Blocking reduces effective throughput.
M/D/1 has exponential service times.
The P-K formula applies to M/G/1.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8. False: 4, 7.

Little's law applies to stable conservative systems. M/D/1 has deterministic service.

prompt: Which statements are true for application protocol stacks? (6p)
options: Time-critical applications need low latency and low jitter.
TCP is reliable but can add retransmission delay.
QUIC can provide secure, low-latency transport.
Non-critical applications can tolerate some delay.
All applications require a global IP address on every sensor.
UDP has no built-in reliability.
The transport protocol is always the same for all applications.
Application requirements influence protocol choice.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8. False: 5, 7.

Sensors behind a gateway may not need a global IP. Protocol choice depends on latency, reliability and energy requirements.

prompt: Which statements are true for vehicular/ad-hoc applications? (6p)
options: Vehicle-to-vehicle communication can use ad-hoc links.
Geocast can warn vehicles in a relevant area.
URLLC can support low-latency vehicle control.
Vehicular networks always require a central base station.
Position-based routing can use GPS coordinates.
DTN is suitable for time-critical braking control.
Multi-hop forwarding can extend coverage.
AODV is a reactive routing protocol.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8. False: 4, 6.

VANETs can be infrastructure-less or use infrastructure. DTN is not suitable for hard real-time braking.

prompt: Which statements are true for energy-efficient MAC? (6p)
options: Duty cycling lets a device sleep between transmissions.
Contention-based MAC can waste energy on collisions.
Scheduling can reduce collisions and energy use.
A device should always keep its radio on to save energy.
DRX is a cellular power-saving mechanism.
Class A LoRa devices have short receive windows.
Energy consumption is irrelevant for battery-powered sensors.
Beacons can help synchronize sleep schedules.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8. False: 4, 7.

Sleeping radios save energy; keeping the radio on wastes battery. DRX and beaconing help coordination.

prompt: Which statements are good principles for system design scenarios? (6p)
options: Start from application requirements such as latency and reliability.
Choose a network architecture that matches coverage and mobility.
Always choose the technology with the highest peak data rate.
Consider energy, maintenance and cost.
Use a backhaul link to reach the core/cloud.
Ignore security and privacy if the budget is low.
Use edge/fog computing when latency matters.
A design should explain why the chosen protocols fit the scenario.
solution:
True: 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8. False: 3, 6.

The highest peak rate is not always appropriate. Requirements, energy, cost, security and backhaul must be balanced.

prompt:
A server has Poisson arrivals with λ = 5 requests/s and exponential service with mean 0.1 s. Model it as M/M/1.

  1. What is μ?
  2. What is the utilization?
  3. What is the average number in the system?
  4. What is the average response time?
solution:
Solution

μ = 1/0.1 = 10 requests/s; ρ = 5/10 = 0.5.

N = ρ/(1−ρ) = 0.5/0.5 = 1 request.

T = N/λ = 1/5 = 0.2 s.

prompt:
Use the same λ = 5 requests/s and mean service time 0.1 s, but now service times are deterministic (M/D/1).

  1. What is the utilization?
  2. What is the average number in the system?
  3. What is the average response time?

Packets arrive as a Poisson process with λ = 2 packets/s.

  1. What is P(exactly 3 arrivals in 1 s)?
  2. What is P(0 arrivals in 2 s)?
  3. What is the expected number in 3 s?
solution:
Solution

P(3 in 1 s) = e−22³/3! ≈ 0.1804.

P(0 in 2 s) = e−4 ≈ 0.0183.

Expected number in 3 s = 2·3 = 6.

prompt:
Three devices use slotted ALOHA with transmission probabilities 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 in each slot, independently. A slot succeeds only with exactly one transmission.

  1. What is P(empty)?
  2. What is P(exactly one)?
  3. What is P(collision)?

A finite queue has P(0)=0.1, P(1)=0.2, P(2)=0.3 and P(3)=0.4. Arrivals are λ=3 requests/s and blocked when the system is full. Service rate is μ=4 requests/s.

  1. What is the average number in the system?
  2. What is the blocking probability?
  3. What is the effective throughput?
  4. What is the average response time for accepted requests?
solution:
Solution

prompt:
A 100 kbit message is sent to Mars at 2 Mbit/s. The distance is 225 million km, and the signal speed is 3·108 m/s.

  1. What is the propagation delay?
  2. What is the transmission time?
  3. What is the total one-way delay?
solution:
Solution

Propagation = 225·109/3·108 = 750 s.

Transmission = 100,000/2,000,000 = 0.05 s.

Total ≈ 750.05 s, i.e. about 12.5 minutes.

prompt: Scenario: A city district wants high-density public WiFi and 5G for residents, cameras and buses. Design the access, backhaul and back-end architecture.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use WiFi 6/7 access points and 5G small cells for high-density coverage.
  • Connect access points via fiber/radio backhaul to a core network.
  • Use edge servers for latency-sensitive video analytics; cloud for storage.
  • Separate public, camera and bus traffic with VLANs/slicing and security policies.
  • Plan capacity and interference; use licensed spectrum for 5G.

prompt: Scenario: Scania tests truck platooning with one leader and up to four followers. The trucks need low-latency, reliable communication. Propose a network design.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use 5G URLLC or a dedicated short-range radio link for platoon control.
  • Use V2V links between trucks and a cellular backhaul to the fleet backend.
  • Keep safety-critical control local/edge to minimize latency.
  • Add redundancy and fail-safe behavior for connectivity loss.
  • Use mMTC/eMBB for non-critical telemetry and video.

prompt: Scenario: A rural village needs Internet access for schools, a clinic and sensors. Terrestrial fiber is too expensive. Design a solution.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use satellite backhaul (Starlink/VSAT) for the village gateway.
  • Distribute access with WiFi/mesh and LPWAN for sensors.
  • Place an edge/cache server for educational content and clinic data.
  • Use solar/battery power and monitor energy use.
  • Plan for high satellite latency and possible outages; DTN for non-critical data.

prompt: Scenario: A Sámi community wants to track reindeer and get basic Internet at remote camps. Connectivity is poor. Propose an architecture.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use LPWAN tags and a gateway for reindeer position updates.
  • Use satellite backhaul for the gateway/Internet access.
  • Use DTN/store-and-forward for intermittent links and non-critical data.
  • Use solar/battery power at remote sites.
  • Provide WiFi at camps for email/web; prioritize basic services.

prompt: Scenario: An underwater habitat needs local communication and data transfer to the surface. Design an underwater network with sensors and AUVs.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use acoustic links for long-range sensor data and JANUS for interoperability.
  • Use optical links for short high-rate AUV transfers.
  • AUVs act as mobile data mules to surface gateways (DTN).
  • Use acoustic localization/ranging because GPS is unavailable.
  • Surface gateway uses satellite/coastal backhaul to the cloud.

prompt: Scenario: A future Mars base needs Internet-like communication with Earth and local communication between habitats and rovers. Design the network.
solution:
Example solution

  • Use deep-space radio/optical links with DTN and LTP.
  • Use space relays to handle occultation and long delays.
  • Build a local Mars network (WiFi/mesh) for habitats and rovers.
  • Use store-and-forward and scheduled contacts; TCP is not suitable end-to-end.
  • Plan for solar power and high latency; use local caching/edge computing.
